title: Lesson 27: Cost Control, Caching, Model Tiers, Budget Caps, and Spend Dashboards
description: A working agent is cheaper to build than to keep. Lesson 26 stopped a single tenant from blowing the monthly bill in an afternoon; this lesson turns the bill itself into a number you manage. It covers the three cost levers in order: caching so you never pay twice for the same answer, model tiers and routing so you only pay frontier prices when a task actually needs them, and budget caps with spend dashboards so a surprise bill becomes an early-warning system instead. A worked example runs the arithmetic on a real agent workload, and the Fortress angle shows a hybrid two-tier stack doing all three at once.

questions.question: In what order should the cost levers be applied, and why?
options: Cap, then cache, then route, since a budget ceiling stops overspending right away
Cache, then route across tiers, then cap and watch, since the first two set the amount spent
Watch first, then cap, then route, since a spend dashboard shows exactly where the money went
Route first, then watch, then cache, since per-token pricing gaps are the single biggest lever
questions.explanation: Caching and routing reduce how much is spent before any cap matters; a dashboard only reports where the money went, so reaching for it first leaves the bill unchanged.

questions.question: Why can a cheaper model end up costing more?
options: A lower price per token always lowers the total bill no matter what the task actually involves
Cheaper models can never be called as often as a frontier model can be
Cheaper models bill in a separate currency that is significantly harder to track
A lower price per token can raise cost per task when its mistakes force retries or review
questions.explanation: The metric that matters is cost per completed task, not cost per token, because a cheap model that makes mistakes can cost more downstream than the frontier model would have.

questions.question: What is the risk of a semantic cache with a loose similarity threshold?
options: It can return an answer that only resembles the question, which is a correctness bug
It stores every cached answer twice, roughly doubling the storage cost of the cache itself
It refuses almost every cache hit, calling the model for each request again
It slows the first call in each window while the cached prefix is written
questions.explanation: A semantic cache decides a hit by embedding similarity, so a loose threshold starts serving answers that merely resemble the question, which makes the threshold a correctness decision and not only a cost one.
